chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: Every construction uses only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and every one is followed by its reason: which triangles are congruent, and by which condition. The chapter opens with a pair of eyes drawn with two arcs and ends with tilings, where counting and colouring decide what is possible.

points.title: Try first, name later
points.text: The hook video leaves the eyes question open: where must the compass point go so that both arcs meet at the corners? The perpendicular bisector is named only after the student has found the two centres.

points.title: Every step has a reason
points.text: Each construction is justified by congruent triangles: SSS for the bisector, the copied angle and the angle bisector, SAS for the right angle at the midpoint, and an equilateral triangle for 60°.

points.title: Concept, then practice, topic by topic
points.text: Each idea gets its own topic: one video per concept, a closing practice concept (with a tool where the manipulation is the idea), then the book's Figure it Out questions in their own topic, one question and one video per concept.

points.title: Counting and colouring decide tilings
points.text: A 2 × 1 tile covers two squares, and one black and one white on a chessboard colouring. An odd count, or unequal black and white counts, shows a region can never be tiled.

concepts.concept_name: Two arcs make an eye

content.text:
6 Constructions and Tilings
6.1 Geometric Constructions
Eyes
Do you recall the 'Eyes' construction we did in Grade 6?
Of course, eyes can be drawn freehand, but we wanted to construct them so that the lower arc and upper arc of each eye look symmetrical. We relied on our spatial estimation to determine the two centres, A and B (see the figure), from which we drew the lower arc and upper arc respectively.
The arcs define a line XY that 'supports' the drawing though it is not part of the final figure. We can start with this supporting line and systematically find the centres A and B.

3. Keep this question in mind: the next topic finds the two centres exactly and names the line through them.

concepts.concept_name: Finding the centres A and B

content.text:
For the eye to be symmetrical, or for the supporting line to be the line of symmetry, the upper and lower arcs should have the same radius. In other words, we must have AX = BX. Since AX = AY and BX = BY, this means AX = AY = BX = BY.
How do we find such A and B?
From X and Y, draw arcs above and below XY, with the same radii. The two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, give us A and B, respectively.
Use this to construct an eye.
Join A and B with a line. Where does AB intersect XY, and what is the angle formed between them?
We observe that AB passes through the midpoint of XY, and is also perpendicular to it.
A division of a line, or any geometrical object, into two identical parts is called bisection. A line that bisects a given line and is perpendicular to it, is called the perpendicular bisector.

content.text:
1. Predict first: if an arc is centred at A and passes through X and Y, what must be true of AX and AY?
2. Arcs of one radius from X and from Y meet at a point A above XY and at a point B below XY; then AX = AY = BX = BY.
3. With A as centre draw the lower arc through X and Y; with B as centre draw the upper arc. The eye is symmetrical about XY.
4. Join A and B: the line AB passes through the midpoint of XY and makes a right angle with it. Such a line is called the perpendicular bisector of XY.

content.text:
Worked example: XY is a line segment. Using only a ruler and a compass, find the centres A and B for the two arcs of an eye with corners X and Y, and draw the eye.
1. Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY.
2. With centre X, draw an arc above XY and an arc below XY.
3. With centre Y and the same radius, draw arcs that cut the first two arcs.
4. Name the meeting point above XY as A and the one below XY as B. Then AX = AY = BX = BY.
5. With centre A and radius AX, draw the lower arc from X to Y.
6. With centre B and the same radius, draw the upper arc from X to Y. The two arcs make the eye.
Answer: A and B are the meeting points of equal arcs from X and Y; the arc centred at A is the lower arc and the arc centred at B is the upper arc

concepts.concept_name: Why AB is the perpendicular bisector

content.text:
Will the line joining the two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, always be the perpendicular bisector of XY, i.e., when XY is of any length, and the arcs are drawn using a radius of any length?
This can be answered through congruence. Let us consider a line segment XY. Find points A and B such that AX = AY = BX = BY. Draw the lines AB, AX, AY, BX and BY. Let O be the point of intersection between AB and XY.
Which two triangles should be congruent for AB to be the perpendicular bisector of XY (that is, O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY)?
If we show that ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY, then OX = OY, and ∠AOX = ∠AOY because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles. Since ∠AOX and ∠AOY together form a straight angle, we have ∠AOX + ∠AOY = 180°. Thus, ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°. This establishes that O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY.
In ΔAOX and ΔAOY, we already know that AX = AY, and AO is common to both triangles.
If we can show that ∠XAO = ∠YAO then, by the SAS congruence condition, we can conclude that the triangles are congruent.
To show this, we observe that ΔABX ≅ ΔABY. This is so because AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common to both the triangles.
Thus, we have ∠XAB = ∠YAB, or ∠XAO = ∠YAO because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles.
Hence, AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.

lines: Will the line joining the two points at which the arcs meet, above and below XY, always be the perpendicular bisector of XY, i.e., when XY is of any length, and the arcs are drawn using a radius of any length?

This can be answered through congruence. Let us consider a line segment XY. Find points A and B such that AX = AY = BX = BY. Draw the lines AB, AX, AY, BX and BY. Let O be the point of intersection between AB and XY.
Which two triangles should be congruent for AB to be the perpendicular bisector of XY (that is, O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY)?

If we show that ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY, then OX = OY, and ∠AOX = ∠AOY because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles. Since ∠AOX and ∠AOY together form a straight angle, we have ∠AOX + ∠AOY = 180°. Thus, ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°. This establishes that O is the midpoint of XY and AB is perpendicular to XY.
In ΔAOX and ΔAOY, we already know that AX = AY, and AO is common to both triangles.
If we can show that ∠XAO = ∠YAO then, by the SAS congruence condition, we can conclude that the triangles are congruent.
To show this, we observe that ΔABX ≅ ΔABY. This is so because AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common to both the triangles.
Thus, we have ∠XAB = ∠YAB, or ∠XAO = ∠YAO because they are corresponding parts of congruent triangles.
Hence, AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.

content.text:
1. Predict first: which pair of triangles, if congruent, would give OX = OY and a right angle at O?
2. Step one: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, since AX = AY, BX = BY and AB is common. So ∠XAO = ∠YAO.
3. Step two: ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS, since AX = AY, ∠XAO = ∠YAO and AO is common. So OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY.
4. The two angles at O make a straight angle of 180°, so each is 90°.

content.text:
Worked example: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at O. Prove that O is the midpoint of XY and that AB is perpendicular to XY.
1. In ΔABX and ΔABY: AX = AY, BX = BY, and AB is common. So ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by the SSS condition.
2. Corresponding parts are equal, so ∠XAB = ∠YAB, that is, ∠XAO = ∠YAO.
3. In ΔAOX and ΔAOY: AX = AY, ∠XAO = ∠YAO, and AO is common. So ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by the SAS condition.
4. Corresponding parts are equal, so OX = OY: O is the midpoint of XY.
5. Also ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and together they make a straight angle of 180°.
6. So each of ∠AOX and ∠AOY is half of 180°, which is 90°.
Answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY

concepts.concept_name: Every point equally far from X and Y lies on AB

content.text:
We can have eyes of different shapes. How do we get these different shapes? Try!
One way is to choose two other points C and D such that CX = CY = DX = DY. An eye of a different shape can be drawn using these points.
Will C and D lie on the perpendicular bisector AB?
The points C and D are at the same distance from both X and Y. We have just seen that joining any two such points gives the perpendicular bisector of XY. Since XY has only one perpendicular bisector, which is the line AB, the points C and D must lie on the line AB.
Justify the following statement using the facts that we have established. Any point that has the same distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
Thus, eyes of different shapes can be drawn by suitably choosing different pairs of points on the perpendicular bisector as centres to construct the upper and lower arcs of the eyes.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a new point C has CX = CY. Will it lie on the line AB, or somewhere else?
2. Pair C with A, or with B on the other side: the line through two points that are each equally far from X and Y is the perpendicular bisector of XY, by the same SSS then SAS proof.
3. XY has only one perpendicular bisector, so that line is AB, and C is on it.
4. Different pairs of centres on AB give eyes of different shapes.

content.text:
Worked example: A point P is the same distance from X and Y, that is, PX = PY. Justify that P lies on the perpendicular bisector AB of XY.
1. If P is on the same side of XY as A, pair P with B; otherwise pair P with A. Say we pair P with B.
2. Then PX = PY and BX = BY, so P and B are each equally far from X and Y.
3. In ΔPBX and ΔPBY: PX = PY, BX = BY, and PB is common, so ΔPBX ≅ ΔPBY by SSS.
4. So ∠XPB = ∠YPB, and if PB meets XY at O, then ΔPOX ≅ ΔPOY by SAS (PX = PY, equal angles at P, PO common). So OX = OY and the angles at O are 90°.
5. So the line PB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
6. XY has only one perpendicular bisector, the line AB, so P lies on AB.
Answer: The line through P and B is the perpendicular bisector of XY (SSS, then SAS); XY has only one perpendicular bisector, so P lies on AB

concepts.concept_name: Practice: find points equally far from X and Y

content.text:
Arcs of the same radius from X and from Y meet at points equally far from X and Y.
The line through two such points cuts XY in half at a right angle: SSS, then SAS.
Every point equally far from X and Y lies on this one line.

tool_config.title: Equal Distance Finder
tool_config.idea: Every point that is the same distance from X and Y lies on one straight line: the perpendicular bisector of XY. The student discovers the line by placing points, not by being told.
tool_config.screen: A segment XY on a grid; a draggable point P with live distances PX and PY; a Drop button that leaves a dot where PX equals PY; a toggle that draws the line through the dropped dots and marks its angle with XY.
student_does: Drag P until PX and PY read the same, then drop a dot.
Drop at least five such dots, above and below XY.
Predict the shape the dots make before turning on the line.
Check where the line meets XY and the angle it makes.
challenges: XY of 6 cm: drop five equal-distance points.
Find the equal-distance point that lies on XY itself (the midpoint).
Find two equal-distance points 5 cm from X and Y (one on each side).
XY turned slanting: drop equal-distance points again.
Test a point 4 cm from X and 5 cm from Y: is it on the line?
Say the angle between the line and XY (90°).
feedback: A dropped dot where PX and PY differ is refused, with both distances shown in red.
When five dots line up, the line appears and the right angle mark flashes at the midpoint.
A point off the line shows which of X and Y it is nearer to.
tool_config.done_when: Six challenges done, with the line drawn and the 90° named.

hint_ladder.text: What must be true of PX and PY for a dot to be accepted?
Find the midpoint first, then look for equal-distance points straight above and below it.
Keep P on the line through the midpoint at a right angle to XY and watch the two distances.
All equal-distance points lie on the perpendicular bisector: through the midpoint, at 90° to XY.

Keep it uncluttered: one main idea per frame, a single clear focal object, generous white space around it, large readable labels, nothing decorative that does not teach. XY horizontal across the middle; four arc crossings stacked on one vertical line through the middle, generous white space left and right.

Exact mathematical structure:
- A horizontal dark segment XY in the middle of the frame, dots and labels X (left) and Y (right).
- Four green (#009E73) dots on a vertical line through the midpoint of XY: two above XY at different heights and two below XY at different heights.
- At each green dot, two short grey (#6B7280) arc pieces cross, one centred at X and one centred at Y, of the same radius for that dot; the four dots use four different radii, all more than half of XY. That is 8 short arc pieces in all.
- A thin dashed reddish purple (#CC79A7) vertical line through all four green dots, crossing XY at its midpoint with a small square right angle mark.
- One short caption line at the bottom of the frame.

Visible text:
- X
- Y
- Equally far from X and Y

Critical rejection conditions:
- a green dot that is not on the reddish purple line, or other than 4 green dots
- other than 8 arc pieces, or a pair of arcs crossing at a point with no green dot
- the line not meeting XY at its midpoint
- any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
- any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
- any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
- a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number

Student takeaway: Every point equally far from X and Y sits on one line that cuts XY in half at a right angle.

media.title: How do we find the two centres of an eye's arcs?
media.context: Constructions and Tilings. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A line segment X Y holds the two corners of an eye. Equal arcs from X and from Y meet above and below the segment, and those two meeting points become the centres of the eye's arcs. Keeko's doubt, a smaller arc from Y, is tested and struck out.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: a centre for an even eye must be the same distance from both corners, and equal arcs from X and Y meet exactly at such a place. Watch for students who change the radius between X and Y.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

final_answer.value: A and B are the meeting points of equal arcs from X and Y; the arc centred at A is the lower arc and the arc centred at B is the upper arc

maths_rules: Same radius r from X and from Y, with r more than half of XY, so that the arcs meet; arcs above and below XY.
The meeting point above XY is A, the one below is B; AX = AY = BX = BY = r.
The arc with centre A and radius AX, from X to Y, is the lower arc; the arc with centre B and the same radius is the upper arc.
Slip: radii r from X and s from Y with s smaller than r give a point P with PX = r and PY = s, so PX is not equal to PY and no arc from P passes through both X and Y.
video_script.design: One idea: equal arcs from both corners fix each centre. The segment X Y stays the whole video. Keeko's doubt is a smaller arc from Y.

media.title: Why does the line through the centres cut XY in half at a right angle?
media.context: Constructions and Tilings. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two points A and B are the same distance from X and from Y. Two pairs of congruent triangles show that the line A B meets X Y at its middle point and at a right angle. Keeko's doubt, that the triangles are congruent because they look the same, is broken by naming a rule.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: first side side side gives equal angles at A, then side angle side gives equal sides and equal angles at O. Watch for students who call triangles congruent because they look alike.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: Why does the line through the centres cut XY in half at a right angle?
items: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child has seen that joining the two meeting points seems to cut X Y in half at a right angle, but has not yet proved it.

interaction_points.prompt: Is O the middle of X Y, and does eigh B stand straight on it?
interaction_points.answer: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY
covers: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at

source: Points A and B satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at
video_script.why: The child has seen that joining the two meeting points seems to cut X Y in half at a right angle, but has not yet proved it.
video_script.substitution: Two pairs of congruent triangles carry the proof: first the two big triangles on A B, then the two small triangles at O.
video_script.anchor: Points A and B with AX = AY = BX = BY, and the line AB meeting the segment XY at O.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko calls the two small triangles at O congruent because they look the same, without naming a rule or showing three equal parts.
video_script.payoff_line: Eigh B is the perpendicular bisector of X Y

final_answer.value: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS; so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°: AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY
final_answer.spoken: eigh B is the perpendicular bisector of X Y, O is its midpoint, and each angle at O is ninety degrees

never_show: the word bisector before the answer line
maths_rules: Given AX = AY and BX = BY; AB is common to triangles ABX and ABY, so triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS.
Corresponding parts are equal, so angle XAB = angle YAB, that is angle XAO = angle YAO, because O lies on AB.
In triangles AOX and AOY: AX = AY, angle XAO = angle YAO, AO is common, so they are congruent by SAS.
So OX = OY (O is the midpoint of XY) and angle AOX = angle AOY.
Angle AOX + angle AOY = 180 degrees (straight angle), and the two are equal, so each is 180 / 2 = 90 degrees.
video_script.design: One idea: two congruences in a chain. Triangles ABX and ABY by SSS give the equal angles at A. Triangles AOX and AOY by SAS give the midpoint and the right angles. Keeko's doubt is that looking alike is enough.

media.title: Is a point equally far from X and Y on the bisector?
media.context: Constructions and Tilings. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A point P is the same distance from X and from Y. Triangles with the point B of the perpendicular bisector show that the line P B is itself the perpendicular bisector, so P lies on it. Keeko's doubt, that P can only be the middle point O, is broken by moving P along the line.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: pair P with a point of the bisector, use the earlier chain of congruent triangles, and use that a segment has only one perpendicular bisector. Watch for students who think an equidistant point must be the midpoint.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: Is a point equally far from X and Y on the bisector?
items: A point P is the same distance from X and Y, that is, PX = P

video_script.why: The child has seen that points on the perpendicular bisector are equally far from X and Y, but has not shown the other way round.
video_script.substitution: Pair P with the point B of the perpendicular bisector, repeat the two congruences from the last proof, and then use that a segment has one perpendicular bisector only.
video_script.anchor: A point P with PX = PY, and the perpendicular bisector AB of XY with the point B on it.
video_script.wrong_answer: P must be the middle point O
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks a point the same distance from X and Y can only be the middle point O of X Y, so P high above the segment could not qualify.
video_script.payoff_line: P lies on the line eigh B, the perpendicular bisector of X Y

final_answer.value: P lies on AB, the perpendicular bisector of XY
final_answer.spoken: P lies on the line eigh B, the perpendicular bisector of X Y

never_show: the word lies before the answer line
maths_rules: Given PX = PY. B is a point of the perpendicular bisector AB of XY, so BX = BY.
In triangles PBX and PBY: PX = PY, BX = BY, PB common, so triangle PBX is congruent to triangle PBY by SSS.
So angle XPB = angle YPB. If PB meets XY at O, triangles POX and POY: PX = PY, equal angles at P, PO common, so congruent by SAS.
So OX = OY and angle POX = angle POY = 90 degrees, so PB is a perpendicular bisector of XY.
A segment has only one perpendicular bisector, so line PB is the line AB, and P lies on AB.
video_script.design: One idea: the earlier chain of congruences, run with P in place of A. The last step uses that a segment has only one perpendicular bisector. Keeko's doubt is that an equidistant point must be the midpoint.

concepts.concept_name: Steps to construct the perpendicular bisector

content.text:
Construction of Perpendicular Bisector
Given a line segment XY, how do we draw its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass?
We have seen that joining any two points, one above XY and one below, that are at equal distances from X and Y, gives the perpendicular bisector of XY. This gives a method to construct the perpendicular bisector.
1. Taking some fixed radius, from X and then Y, construct two sufficiently long arcs above XY. Name the point where the arcs meet as A.
2. Using the same radius, from X and then Y, construct two sufficiently long arcs below XY. Name the point where the arcs meet as B.
3. AB is the required perpendicular bisector.
Thus, the perpendicular bisector can be constructed using the simplest geometric tools, an unmarked ruler and a compass. We will use only these two tools for all the other geometric constructions in this chapter, unless there is a need for drawing lines of specific lengths in standard units.
This method of constructing the perpendicular bisector is not only geometrically exact but also a practical way to construct it accurately.
This method to find the midpoint of a line segment is more accurate than measuring the length using a marked scale.

content.text:
1. Predict first: what is the smallest radius that still lets the arcs from X and Y meet?
2. Step 1: with a radius more than half of XY, draw arcs from X and from Y above XY; they meet at A.
3. Step 2: with the same radius, draw arcs from X and from Y below XY; they meet at B.
4. Step 3: join A and B with the ruler. AB is the perpendicular bisector, and it meets XY at the midpoint O.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a line segment XY. Construct its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and mark the midpoint of XY.
1. Open the compass to a radius more than half of XY, so that the arcs will meet.
2. With centre X, draw a long arc above XY. With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc above XY that cuts it. Name the meeting point A.
3. Keep the same radius. With centres X and Y, draw two arcs below XY that cut each other at B.
4. Join A and B with the ruler. AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY.
5. Mark O where AB crosses XY. O is the midpoint of XY, and ∠AOX = 90°.
6. Reason: AX = AY and BX = BY, so ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS and then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS.
Answer: AB, the line through the two meeting points of equal arcs, is the perpendicular bisector; it meets XY at its midpoint O

tool_config.idea: Two arcs of the same radius, more than half of AB, from A and from B cross at two points; the line through them is the perpendicular bisector. A radius that is too small gives no crossing.

student_does: Set a radius and draw an arc from A.
Draw an arc from B with the same radius and see whether they cross.
Join the two crossing points with the ruler.
Read the check panel: the two halves and the angle.
challenges: AB of 5 cm: construct its perpendicular bisector.
AB of 5 cm with radius 2 cm: see why the arcs do not meet.
AB of 9.5 cm: construct the bisector and find the midpoint.
AB slanting at 30°: construct the bisector.
Arcs of 4 cm from A and 3 cm from B: is the line through the crossings still the bisector?
Mark points 4 cm and 6 cm from both A and B on the bisector.
feedback: A radius of half AB or less shows the arcs missing each other, with the gap highlighted.
Different radii from A and B give a line that misses the midpoint; the two halves show unequal lengths.
A correct construction shows both halves equal and the 90° mark.

maths_rules: Opening r with r more than half of XY, so that arcs from X and from Y meet.
Arcs of radius r from X and Y above XY meet at A; arcs of the same radius r below XY meet at B; AX = AY = BX = BY = r.
Line AB meets XY at O; triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS, and triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS, so OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees.
Slip: with the opening less than half of XY, the arcs from X and Y stop short of each other and do not meet, so no point A exists.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q1: When constructing the perpendicular bisector, is it necessary to have the same radius for the arcs above and below XY? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer. [Hint 1: Any point that is of the same distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector. Hint 2: We can draw the whole line if any two of its points are known.]
1. Construct: arcs of radius r from X and Y above XY meet at A, so AX = AY.
2. Arcs of a different radius s from X and Y below XY meet at B, so BX = BY.
3. A is equally far from X and Y, so A lies on the perpendicular bisector. B is equally far from X and Y, so B lies on it too.
4. Why: ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS (AX = AY, BX = BY, AB common), so ∠XAO = ∠YAO; then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS (AX = AY, equal angles at A, AO common), so OX = OY and ∠AOX = ∠AOY = 90°.
5. Two points fix a whole line, so AB is the perpendicular bisector.
Answer: No. The radius above may differ from the radius below; A and B are each equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and two points fix the line

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q2: Is it necessary to construct the pairs of arcs above and below XY? Instead, can we construct both the pairs of arcs on the same side of XY? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
1. Construct: arcs of radius r from X and Y above XY meet at A.
2. Arcs of a larger radius s from X and Y, also above XY, meet at a second point P. The radii must differ, or the arcs meet at A again.
3. AX = AY and PX = PY, so A and P are each equally far from X and Y.
4. Why: by SSS, ΔAPX ≅ ΔAPY (AX = AY, PX = PY, AP common), so line AP makes equal angles with AX and AY; then SAS on the triangles at the meeting point O gives OX = OY and two 90° angles.
5. So the line AP, extended to cross XY, is the perpendicular bisector.
Answer: No. Both pairs can be on the same side if the two radii are different; each meeting point is equally far from X and Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector (SSS, then SAS), and the line through them, extended, is the perpendicular bisector

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (perpendicular bisector), Q3: While constructing one pair of intersecting arcs, is it necessary that we use the same radii for both of them? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
1. Construct: an arc of radius r from X and an arc of a different radius s from Y meet at a point P.
2. Then PX = r and PY = s, so PX ≠ PY.
3. Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equally far from X and Y: if Q is on it and QO meets XY at O, then ΔQOX ≅ ΔQOY by SAS (OX = OY, ∠QOX = ∠QOY = 90°, QO common), so QX = QY.
4. P is not equally far from X and Y, so P is not on the perpendicular bisector.
5. So a line through P is not the perpendicular bisector.
Answer: Yes. Within one pair the two arcs must have the same radius; otherwise the meeting point is not equally far from X and Y, and every point of the perpendicular bisector is (SAS), so it would not lie on the perpendicular bisector

maths_rules: Radius r from X and from Y above XY, r more than half of XY, meets at A: AX = AY = r.
A different radius s from X and from Y below XY, s more than half of XY, meets at B: BX = BY = s.
Triangle ABX is congruent to triangle ABY by SSS (AX = AY, BX = BY, AB common), so angle XAO = angle YAO where AB meets XY at O.
Triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS (AX = AY, equal angles at A, AO common), so OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees.
A and B are each equally far from X and Y, and two points fix one line, so line AB is the perpendicular bisector.
video_script.design: One idea: the lower arcs may have a different radius from the upper arcs, because each meeting point is equally far from X and Y on its own. The construction of the book's example is repeated, and the same two congruences explain it.

concepts.concept_name: Construct a 90° angle at a given point

content.text:
Construction of a 90° Angle at a Given Point
Can we extend the method of constructing the perpendicular bisector to construct a 90° angle at any point on a line? Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle at point O.
Find a segment of this line for which O is the midpoint.
Extend the line on either side of O. Using a compass, mark two points X and Y at equal distance from O, so that O is the midpoint of XY.
The perpendicular bisector of XY will pass through O and is perpendicular to the given line.
In this case, do we need to draw two pairs of intersecting arcs to get the perpendicular bisector of XY?
No, we don't. We already have one point, O, lying on the perpendicular bisector.

content.text:
1. Predict first: we already know one point of the perpendicular bisector. How many more points do we need?
2. With centre O, cut the line at X and Y, so that OX = OY and O is the midpoint of XY.
3. With a larger radius, draw arcs from X and Y on one side; they meet at A. Then AX = AY.
4. Join OA. ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS, so ∠AOX = ∠AOY, and they make 180°, so each is 90°.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O using only a ruler and a compass, and say why the angle is 90°.
1. With centre O and any radius, draw arcs that cut the line at X and at Y. Then OX = OY.
2. Open the compass wider than OX. With centre X, draw an arc above the line.
3. With centre Y and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at A. Then AX = AY.
4. Join O and A. ∠AOX is the required 90° angle.
5. Reason: in ΔAOX and ΔAOY, AX = AY, OX = OY, and AO is common, so ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS.
6. So ∠AOX = ∠AOY. Together they make 180°, so each is 90°.
Answer: ∠AOX = 90°, since ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS and the two equal angles make a straight angle

concepts.concept_name: Steps to bisect an angle, and why they work

content.text:
We will now develop a general method to bisect any angle. Consider an angle ∠XOY.
We can bisect it if we can draw two congruent triangles ΔOBC and ΔOAC as shown in the figure. Then ∠BOC = ∠AOC.
How do we construct these congruent triangles, given the angle?
If A and B are marked such that OA = OB, and if C is chosen such that BC = AC, then by the SSS congruence condition, ΔOBC ≅ ΔOAC. So we can bisect an angle as follows.
Steps for Angle Bisection
1. Mark points A and B such that OA = OB.
2. Choosing any sufficiently long radius, cut arcs from A and B, keeping the radius same. Mark the point of intersection as C.
3. OC bisects ∠AOB.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw any angle ∠XOY. Bisect it using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the two parts are equal.
1. With centre O and any radius, draw an arc that cuts OY at A and OX at B. Then OA = OB.
2. With centre A and a radius long enough for the arcs to meet, draw an arc inside the angle.
3. With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts it at C. Then AC = BC.
4. Join O and C.
5. In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
6. So ∠AOC = ∠BOC, and OC bisects ∠XOY.
Answer: OC bisects ∠XOY, because ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS

concepts.concept_name: A 45° angle and the eight-petal design

content.text:
Angle Bisection for a Design
How do we construct this figure? (Eight equal petals meet at one centre.)
The supporting lines for this figure will look like this.
What is the angle between two adjacent lines?
We need the angle between every pair of adjacent lines to be equal. Since 360° is equally divided into 8 parts, every angle is 45°.
How do we construct a 45° angle using only a ruler and a compass?
We know how to construct a 90° angle. If we can divide it into two equal parts, or bisect it, then we get a 45° angle.
So, a 45° angle can be constructed by first constructing a 90° angle and then bisecting it.

content.text:
1. Predict first: eight lines from one centre, all equally spaced. What angle is between neighbours?
2. The full turn of 360° split into 8 equal angles gives 45° each.
3. Construct 90° at a point on a line, then bisect it to get 45°.
4. Two perpendicular lines and their two bisectors give the eight supporting lines.

content.text:
Worked example: Eight equal petals meet at a centre, along eight equally spaced supporting lines. Find the angle between neighbouring lines, and construct it with a ruler and a compass.
1. The eight angles round the centre are equal and make a full turn of 360°.
2. The full turn of 360° shared by 8 equal angles gives 45° each.
3. Draw a line and mark the centre O on it. Construct a 90° angle at O with equal arcs.
4. Bisect the 90° angle: arcs from O cut the two arms at A and B, then equal arcs from A and B meet at C. OC makes 45° with each arm (SSS).
5. Extend the two arms and the bisector through O, and bisect one more right angle; this gives four lines, which is eight half-lines from O at 45° to each other.
Answer: Each angle is 45°; construct 90° and bisect it

tool_config.idea: Equal arcs from the vertex and then from the two arm points give a point whose line to the vertex splits the angle into two equal angles (SSS). Halving again gives quarter angles.

student_does: Draw an arc from the vertex cutting both arms.
From the two cut points draw arcs of one radius that cross.
Join the crossing to the vertex and read the two halves.
Halve again to reach quarter angles, or use the result in a design.
challenges: Bisect a 90° angle to get 45°.
Bisect 120° to get 60°.
Bisect 70° and check both halves read 35°.
Make 22.5° by halving twice from 90°.
Decide whether 65.5° can be made by halving from 90° and 60°.
Build the 8-petal design from four 45° lines.
feedback: Arcs from the two arm points with different radii give unequal halves, shown in red.

An unreachable angle such as 65.5° shows the nearest halving results.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q1: Construct at least 4 different angles. Draw their bisectors.
1. Draw four angles of clearly different sizes, for example a small acute angle, a right angle made with equal arcs, a large acute angle and an obtuse angle.
2. For each angle with vertex O: with centre O draw an arc that cuts the arms at A and B, so OA = OB.
3. With one radius, draw arcs from A and from B that meet at C inside the angle.
4. Join OC. It is the bisector, because ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS.
5. Check: fold the paper along OC; the two arms land on each other.
Answer: Each bisector is OC, where OA = OB and AC = BC; ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, so the two halves are equal

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q3

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q3: In Step 2 of angle bisection, if arcs of equal radius are drawn on the other side, so that the arcs from A and B meet at a point C on the far side of the vertex O, outside the angle, will the line OC still be an angle bisector? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
1. Mark A and B on the arms with OA = OB.
2. With a radius larger than OA, draw equal arcs from A and B on the far side of O; they meet at C, with AC = BC.
3. In ΔOAC and ΔOBC: OA = OB, AC = BC, and OC is common.
4. So ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS, and ∠AOC = ∠BOC.
5. Extend CO beyond O to a point D inside ∠AOB. ∠AOD and ∠AOC make a straight angle, and so do ∠BOD and ∠BOC.
6. So ∠AOD = 180° − ∠AOC and ∠BOD = 180° − ∠BOC; these are equal, so the line CO, extended beyond O, bisects ∠AOB.
Answer: Yes. OA = OB, AC = BC and OC is common, so ΔOAC ≅ ΔOBC by SSS and ∠AOC = ∠BOC; their supplements are equal too, so the line CO, extended beyond O, still bisects ∠AOB

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q4: What are the other angles that can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct 65.5° angle?
1. From 180° by halving: 90°. From 90° by halving: 45°, 22.5°, and so on.
2. Sums of these also work, for example 90° + 45° = 135° and 45° + 22.5° = 67.5°.
3. Every angle made this way, doubled enough times, becomes a whole multiple of 45°.
4. 65.5° doubled is 131°, and every further doubling is 131° times a power of 2, which is never a multiple of 45°, because 131 is not divisible by 3 or by 5.
5. So 65.5° cannot be constructed by bisection.
6. Later in this chapter we build a 60° angle; halving it gives 30° and 15°, and sums such as 75°. Those all double into multiples of 15°, and 131° times a power of 2 is not one of them either.
Answer: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made (and, once 60° is built, 30°, 15° and 75°); 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°, or even of 15°

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q6

content.text:
Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q6: Construct the following figure: a square with four equal petals inside it, each petal running from the centre of the square to one corner. How do we construct the petals so that they are of the maximum possible size within a given square?
1. Construct a square: a segment, right angles at both ends, equal sides cut with the compass, and join the fourth side.
2. Find the midpoint of each side by constructing its perpendicular bisector.
3. The two bisectors through opposite midpoints cross at the centre of the square.
4. With centre the midpoint of one side and radius half the side, draw a semicircle inside the square. It passes through the two corners at the ends of that side and through the centre.
5. Do the same from the other three midpoints. Each petal is where two semicircles overlap, from the centre to a corner.
6. These arcs just touch the sides of the square at the corners, so the petals are as large as they can be.
Answer: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q6: Construct the following figure: a square with four equal petals inside it, each petal running from the centre of the square to one corner. How do we construct the petals so that they are of the maximum possible size within a given square?
1. Construct a square: a segment, right angles at both ends, equal sides cut with the compass, and join the fourth side.
2. Find the midpoint of each side by constructing its perpendicular bisector.
3. The two bisectors through opposite midpoints cross at the centre of the square.
4. With centre the midpoint of one side and radius half the side, draw a semicircle inside the square. It passes through the two corners at the ends of that side and through the centre.
5. Do the same from the other three midpoints. Each petal is where two semicircles overlap, from the centre to a corner.
6. These arcs just touch the sides of the square at the corners, so the petals are as large as they can be.
Answer: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

media.context: Constructions and Tilings. Question video: one question from the book, solved step by step by the method of the book's solved example. It opens only after the student has tried the question. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A question from the book asks which other angles bisection can build and whether 65.5 degrees is one of them. Halving and adding give angles such as 135 and 67.5 degrees, and doubling shows that 65.5 degrees can never be reached.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: every angle made by halving and adding doubles into a whole multiple of 45 degrees, and 65.5 degrees does not. Watch for students who try to reach 65.5 degrees by repeated halving of a nearby angle.

interaction_points.prompt: Can you construct an angle of sixty five and a half degrees?
interaction_points.answer: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made; 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°
covers: Figure it Out (angle bisection), Q4

video_script.why: The child can build ninety and forty five degrees and has not yet asked which other angles bisection reaches, or which it cannot reach.
video_script.substitution: The angles are built in the same way as the example in the book, by halving a right angle again and again, and by placing two built angles side by side.
video_script.anchor: What other angles can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct a 65.5 degree angle?
video_script.payoff_line: A sixty five and a half degree angle cannot be built by bisection

final_answer.value: Angles such as 90°, 45°, 22.5°, 135° and 67.5° can be made; 65.5° cannot, because no number of doublings turns it into a multiple of 45°
final_answer.spoken: angles such as ninety, forty five, twenty two and a half, one hundred and thirty five, and sixty seven and a half degrees can be made; sixty five and a half degrees cannot

never_show: the verdict on 65.5 before the answer line
maths_rules: Adding two built angles: 90 + 45 = 135, 45 + 22.5 = 67.5.
Every angle built by halving and adding is a whole multiple of 180 / 2^k, so doubled k times it is a whole multiple of 180, hence of 45.
65.5 x 2 = 131; further doublings give 131 x 2^n. A multiple of 45 needs the factors 3 and 5; 131 is prime, so 131 x 2^n has neither.
Check: 22.5 doubled twice is 90 = 2 x 45 and 67.5 doubled is 135 = 3 x 45, but 131 lies between 90 and 135 and is not a multiple of 45.
video_script.design: One idea: halving and adding only reach angles that double into multiples of 45 degrees. The sixty degree and fifteen degree angles belong to a later topic and are not used here.

final_answer.value: Find the midpoints of the four sides; from each midpoint draw a semicircle of radius half the side inside the square; the four petals run from the centre to the corners and are the largest possible

maths_rules: Square ABCD: right angles at A and B by equal arcs, AD = BC = AB cut with the compass, and D joined to C.
Midpoints P, Q, R, S of AB, BC, CD, DA by perpendicular bisectors; the bisectors through P and R and through Q and S cross at the centre O.
PO = half of AB, because P is the midpoint of AB and PO is perpendicular to AB with O at half the height. PA = PB = half of AB too.
A semicircle with centre P and radius PA, inside the square, passes through A, B and O. The same holds for Q, R and S.
Two neighbouring semicircles, for example from P and from Q, overlap in a petal from O to B. Four such petals run from O to A, B, C and D.
A radius longer than half the side from P would cut the sides of the square beyond the corners, so the arc leaves the square.

concepts.concept_name: Steps to copy an angle

content.text:
Repeating Units and Repeating Angles
Consider a design made of a row of five equal sectors (shapes with two equal straight arms and an arc), alternately pointing down and up, with neighbouring sectors sharing an arm. In this design, there is a single unit repeating itself. To construct this figure, we need to make exact copies of this unit in two different orientations.
In order to make exact copies, all the units must have the same arm lengths and the same angle between the arms. We can ensure equal arm lengths using a compass, but how do we ensure equal angles?
Let us develop a method to create an exact copy of a given angle.
Draw an angle. Create a copy of this angle using only a ruler and compass.
Steps of Construction to Copy an Angle
Draw an arc from A. This gives us three points that form the isosceles triangle ΔABC.
Draw an arc of the same radius from X.
Measure BC using a compass. Transfer this length on the arc from Z to get YZ = BC.
By the SSS congruence condition, ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ. So, ∠A = ∠X.

content.text:
1. Predict first: what must match, besides the arm lengths, for a copy to have the same angle?
2. With centre A, draw an arc that cuts the arms at B and C.
3. Draw a ray from X. With centre X and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts the ray at Z.
4. Open the compass to BC. With centre Z, cut the arc at Y. Join XY. ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, so ∠X = ∠A.

content.text:
Worked example: An angle with vertex A is drawn. Copy it onto a ray from a point X using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the copy is equal.
1. With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the two arms at B and C. Then AB = AC.
2. Draw a ray from X. With centre X and the same radius, draw a long arc that cuts the ray at Z. Then XZ = AB.
3. Open the compass to the length BC.
4. With centre Z and radius BC, cut the arc at Y. Then YZ = BC and XY = AC.
5. Join X and Y.
6. In ΔABC and ΔXYZ: AB = XZ, AC = XY, BC = ZY. So ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, and ∠YXZ = ∠CAB.
Answer: ∠YXZ is a copy of ∠A, because ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS

tool_config.title: Angle Copier
tool_config.idea: Copying an angle means copying an arc and the chord across it: two triangles with three equal sides (SSS) give an equal angle in any position.
tool_config.screen: A given angle and a new ray that can be turned to any direction; a compass that keeps its last radius; steps: arc on the given angle, the same arc on the new ray, measure the chord, transfer the chord; an overlay that lifts the copy onto the original.
student_does: Draw an arc on the given angle and the same arc on the new ray.
Measure the chord across the given arc with the compass.
Transfer that chord to the new arc and draw the second arm.
Lift the copy onto the original to check.
challenges: Copy a 50° angle onto a horizontal ray.
Copy a 110° angle onto a slanting ray.
Copy an angle onto a ray pointing the other way.
Copy an angle twice side by side to double it.
Copy a sector angle along a line to start a sector row.
Copy an angle with a long arm and a short arm.
feedback: A changed radius on the second arc shows the copy too wide or too narrow, in red.
A correct copy lifts exactly onto the original with the SSS triangles shaded.
Arm length changes do not change the readout, which shows that angle does not depend on arm length.
tool_config.done_when: Six challenges done with the copies matching.

hint_ladder.text: Which two lengths do you need to carry from the given angle to the new ray?
Keep the same arc radius on both, then carry the chord length.
Set the compass on the two arc points of the given angle, then cut the new arc with it.
Same arc and same chord give congruent triangles by SSS, so the angles are equal.

maths_rules: An arc with centre A cuts the arms at B and C: AB = AC.
The same radius from X gives a long arc that cuts the ray at Z: XZ = AB, and every point Y on the long arc has XY = AC.
The compass is set to BC; from Z it cuts the long arc at Y: ZY = BC.
Triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY by SSS, so angle YXZ = angle CAB.
Slip: a new radius at X breaks XZ = AB, so the triangles no longer have three equal pairs of sides.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (copying an angle), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (copying an angle), Q1: Construct at least 4 different angles in different orientations without taking any measurement. Make a copy of all these angles.
1. Draw four angles with the ruler only, each in a different direction on the page, for example one opening upwards, one sideways, one downwards and one slanting.
2. For each angle with vertex A: draw an arc from A cutting the arms at B and C.
3. Draw a new ray from a point X, and with the same radius draw an arc from X cutting it at Z.
4. Open the compass to BC, and from Z cut the arc at Y. Join XY.
5. Each copy is equal because ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS. Check by laying tracing paper over both.
Answer: For each angle, equal arcs from A and X and the chord BC moved to ZY give ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SSS, so every copy equals its angle

concepts.concept_name: Copy a corresponding angle to draw a parallel line

content.text:
This procedure to copy an angle finds an important application in constructing parallel lines using only a ruler and compass.
Construction of a Line Parallel to the Given Line
Recall that we constructed equal corresponding angles to get parallel lines.
How do we implement this idea using a ruler and a compass?
Suppose there is a line m to which we need to draw a parallel line. We construct a line l that intersects m. Line l will serve as a transversal to line m and to the line parallel to m that we are going to construct.
Let us choose a point B on l through which we are going to draw the parallel line. This parallel line must make the same corresponding angle, as shown in the figure. This can be done by copying the angle between m and l.
Construct arcs of equal radius from A and B. Transfer the length CD to the arc from F (F is where the arc from B cuts l). These steps give a method to construct a line parallel to the given line.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a transversal crosses two lines. Which angles must be equal for the lines to be parallel?
2. Draw a line l through B that cuts m at A. The angle a between m and l at A is the one to copy.
3. Equal arcs from A and from B; the chord CD at A is transferred to the arc at B, giving E.
4. The line n through B and E makes the same corresponding angle a, so n is parallel to m.

content.text:
Worked example: A line m and a point B not on it are given. Construct a line through B parallel to m using only a ruler and a compass.
1. Draw a line l through B that cuts m at A. l is the transversal.
2. With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts m at C and cuts l at D, on the part of l between A and B.
3. With centre B and the same radius, draw an arc that cuts l at F, on the side of B away from A, as for the matching corner.
4. Open the compass to CD. With centre F, cut the arc at E, on the same side of l as C.
5. Draw the line n through B and E. ΔBFE ≅ ΔADC by SSS, so the angle at B equals the angle at A.
6. These are corresponding angles, so n is parallel to m.
Answer: The line n through B and E, since the copied corresponding angles are equal (SSS), so n ∥ m

maths_rules: Line l through B cuts m at A; l is the transversal.
An arc with centre A cuts m at C and l at D, between A and B: AC = AD.
The same radius with centre B cuts l at F, beyond B, away from A: BF = AD, and every point E on this arc has BE = AC.
The compass is set to CD; with centre F it cuts the arc at E, on the same side of l as C: FE = DC.
Triangle BFE is congruent to triangle ADC by SSS, so angle FBE = angle DAC. These are corresponding angles on the transversal l, so n through B and E is parallel to m.
Slip: E on the other side of l gives the angle in the opposite corner, and the line through B and E is not parallel to m.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (parallel lines), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (parallel lines), Q1: Construct 4 pairs of parallel lines in different orientations.
1. Draw four lines m in different directions: across, up and down, and two slanting ways.
2. For each, mark a point B off the line and draw a transversal l through B cutting m at A.
3. Equal arcs from A and B; the chord CD at A is transferred to the arc at B to give E.
4. Draw n through B and E. ΔADC ≅ ΔBFE by SSS, so the corresponding angles are equal.
5. So each n is parallel to its m.
Answer: Four pairs m and n, each made by copying the corresponding angle at A to B (SSS), so each n ∥ m

concepts.concept_name: Six equilateral triangles round a point

content.text:
Regular Hexagons
Recall that a regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. A regular polygon with 3 sides is an equilateral triangle, and a regular polygon with 4 sides is a square. We have constructed these figures earlier.
Constructing a regular hexagon is within our reach! Can we break a regular hexagon into smaller pieces that can be constructed?
Regular Hexagon and Equilateral Triangles
What happens when we join the 'opposite' points of a regular hexagon? Since a regular hexagon has equal sides and angles, can we expect a figure like this? Will all the triangles in the figure be equilateral triangles?
To answer these questions, we will reverse our approach. Can six congruent equilateral triangles be placed together as in the figure? If yes, will it result in a regular hexagon?
If six congruent equilateral triangles can indeed be placed as shown in the figure, then the sides of the resulting hexagon are equal, and their angles are 60 + 60 = 120° (how?). So what we really need to examine is whether 6 congruent equilateral triangles can fit this way without overlapping and without leaving any gaps around the centre.
We have defined a degree by taking the complete angle around a point to be 360°. So all the angles around the centre should add up to 360°.
Since each angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°, six such angles add up to 360°. Therefore, six congruent triangles can be arranged as shown.

Regular Hexagon and Equilateral Triangles

What happens when we join the 'opposite' points of a regular hexagon? Since a regular hexagon has equal sides and angles, can we expect a figure like this? Will all the triangles in the figure be equilateral triangles?
To answer these questions, we will reverse our approach. Can six congruent equilateral triangles be placed together as in the figure? If yes, will it result in a regular hexagon?

If six congruent equilateral triangles can indeed be placed as shown in the figure, then the sides of the resulting hexagon are equal, and their angles are 60 + 60 = 120° (how?). So what we really need to examine is whether 6 congruent equilateral triangles can fit this way without overlapping and without leaving any gaps around the centre.
We have defined a degree by taking the complete angle around a point to be 360°. So all the angles around the centre should add up to 360°.
Since each angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°, six such angles add up to 360°. Therefore, six congruent triangles can be arranged as shown.

3. The outer sides are all sides of congruent triangles, so they are equal.
4. At each corner of the hexagon two triangle angles meet: 60° + 60° = 120°.

concepts.concept_name: Opposite corners lie on straight lines

content.text: Can you explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines?
content.publication_text: Can you explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines?
lines: Can you explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines?

content.text:
1. Predict first: from A through O to D, how many 60° angles are passed at O?
2. Going round O from OA to OD passes three triangles: 60° + 60° + 60° = 180°.
3. An angle of 180° is a straight angle, so A, O and D lie on one straight line.
4. The same holds for B, O, E and for C, O, F.

Going round O from OA to OD passes three triangles: 60° + 60° + 60° = 180°.

The same holds for B, O, E and for C, O, F.

content.text:
Worked example: In a regular hexagon ABCDEF made of six equilateral triangles round the centre O, explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines.
1. At O, ∠AOB, ∠BOC and ∠COD are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is 60°.
2. ∠AOD = ∠AOB + ∠BOC + ∠COD = 60° + 60° + 60° = 180°.
3. An angle of 180° is a straight angle, so OA and OD point in opposite directions: AOD is a straight line.
4. In the same way ∠BOE = 180° and ∠COF = 180°.
5. So BOE and COF are straight lines too.
Answer: Each of ∠AOD, ∠BOE and ∠COF is three 60° angles, which is 180°, a straight angle

Going anticlockwise from the ray pointing right: a 110° wedge shaded teal (#0072B2), then a 90° wedge shaded amber (#E69F00) with a small square right angle mark, then a 75° wedge shaded teal (#0072B2).
The fourth angle, the gap, is 85°, shaded reddish purple (#CC79A7) with a small angle arc, and labelled 85°.
Each of the three placed wedges carries its own angle label inside it: 110°, 90°, 75°.
To the right, one line of text: 360° − 275° = 85°, with the 85° written in reddish purple (#CC79A7).
Check: 110 + 90 + 75 = 275 and 360 − 275 = 85, so the four angles add to 360°.

maths_rules: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees.
At O, six such angles meet, and 6 x 60 = 360, the full angle round a point, so there is no gap and no overlap.
The six outer sides are sides of congruent triangles, so they are all equal.
At each outer corner two angles of 60 degrees meet, making 60 + 60 = 120 degrees, so all six angles are equal.
Equal sides and equal angles make the outer figure a regular hexagon.

maths_rules: Angles AOB, BOC and COD are angles of equilateral triangles, so each is 60 degrees.
Angle AOD = angle AOB + angle BOC + angle COD = 60 + 60 + 60 = 180 degrees; added in steps: 60 + 60 = 120, 120 + 60 = 180.
An angle of 180 degrees is a straight angle, so OA and OD point in opposite directions and AOD is a straight line.
In the same way angle BOE = 180 degrees and angle COF = 180 degrees, so BOE and COF are straight lines too.

concepts.concept_name: Construct a 60° angle

content.text:
We can construct a regular hexagon more directly if we can construct a 120° angle using a ruler and a compass. How do we do it? This can be done if we can construct a 60° angle.
Construction of a 60° angle
How do we construct a 60° angle? We get a 60° angle if we construct an equilateral triangle! We can use the following steps for this.
Suppose we need a 60° angle at point A on a line segment AX.
Step 1: Construct an arc with centre A and any radius. (It cuts AX at B.)
Step 2: With the same radius, cut another arc from B that meets the first arc. Let C be the point at which the arcs meet. We have ∠CAX = 60°.
Why is ∠CAX = 60°? Is there an equilateral triangle here?

content.text:
1. Predict first: which triangle has every angle equal to 60°?
2. An arc with centre A cuts AX at B; an arc of the same radius from B meets it at C.
3. AB = AC (radii from A) and BA = BC (radii from B), so all three sides are equal.
4. ABC is equilateral, so each angle is 60°, and ∠CAX = ∠CAB = 60°.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
1. Draw a line and mark A on it. Mark X on the line to the right of A.
2. With centre A and any radius, draw a large arc that cuts AX at B.
3. With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60°.
4. With centre C and the same radius, cut the arc again at D. Then ∠DAC = 60°, by the same equilateral triangle reason.
5. Join A and D. ∠DAX = 60° + 60° = 120°.
6. Check: D lies on the side away from X, and the angle between AD and the line on the left is 180° − 120° = 60°.
Answer: ∠DAX = 120°, made of two 60° angles from equilateral triangles

concepts.concept_name: 120° and regular hexagons of a given side

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a regular hexagon with side 4 cm using a ruler and a compass.
1. Open the compass to 4 cm using the ruler, and draw a circle with centre O.
2. Mark a point A on the circle.
3. With centre A and radius 4 cm, cut the circle at B. ΔOAB is equilateral, so ∠AOB = 60°.
4. With centre B, cut the circle at C; with centre C, cut at D; then E and F in the same way.
5. Six angles of 60° at O make 360°, so the sixth step lands back on A.
6. Join A, B, C, D, E, F in order. Every side is 4 cm and every angle is 60° + 60° = 120°.
Answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 4 cm and six angles of 120°

concepts.concept_name: 120° and regular hexagons of a given side

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a regular hexagon with side 5 cm using the 120° construction at each corner.
1. Draw AB = 5 cm with the ruler.
2. At B, construct 120° between BA and a new ray: two 60° steps with equal arcs. Cut the ray at C with BC = 5 cm.
3. At C, construct 120° in the same way, turning the same direction, and cut CD = 5 cm.
4. Repeat at D and E to get E and F with DE = EF = 5 cm.
5. Join F to A. The angles of a regular hexagon add to 6 × 120 = 720 degrees, and FA comes out 5 cm.
6. All six sides are 5 cm and all six angles are 120°.
Answer: ABCDEF, with six sides of 5 cm and six angles of 120°

maths_rules: Compass set to 4 cm with the ruler; circle with centre O; A on the circle.

6 x 60° = 360°, so the next step from F lands back on A.
Each side is 4 cm; each corner angle is 60° + 60° = 120°.

content.text:
Worked example: Construct a 30° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
1. With centre A and any radius, draw an arc that cuts the line at B.
2. With centre B and the same radius, cut the arc at C. Then ∠CAB = 60° (ΔABC is equilateral).
3. Now bisect ∠CAB: with one radius, draw arcs from B and from C that meet at D inside the angle.
4. Join A and D.
5. AB = AC, BD = CD and AD is common, so ΔABD ≅ ΔACD by SSS.
6. So ∠DAB = ∠DAC, and each is half of 60°, which is 30°.
Answer: ∠DAB = 30°: a 60° angle from an equilateral triangle, bisected (SSS)

content.text:

2. Construct a regular hexagon GHIJKL and extend each side both ways.
3. Each angle of the hexagon is 120°; the angle next to it on a straight line is 180° − 120° = 60°.
4. Each point triangle has two 60° base angles, so its third angle is 60° too: it is equilateral.

content.text:
Worked example: A six-pointed star has outer points A, B, C, D, E, F and an inner regular hexagon GHIJKL. Are the six point triangles ΔAGH, ΔBHI, ΔCIJ, ΔDJK, ΔELK and ΔFLG equilateral? Why?
1. The inner figure GHIJKL is a regular hexagon, so each of its angles is 120°.
2. In ΔAGH, side GH is a side of the hexagon, and AG and AH lie along the extended sides LG and IH.
3. ∠AGH and ∠LGH make a straight angle, so ∠AGH = 180° − 120° = 60°.
4. In the same way ∠AHG = 180° − 120° = 60°.
5. The angles of a triangle add to 180°, so ∠GAH = 180° − 60° − 60° = 60°.
6. All three angles are 60°, so ΔAGH is equilateral; the same reasoning works for the other five points.
Answer: Yes. Each base angle is 180° − 120° = 60°, so all three angles are 60° and each point is an equilateral triangle

maths_rules: Construct ∠CAB = 60° with two equal arcs and bisect it, giving ray AD with ∠DAB = 30°.
The first arc from A cuts AD at a point E, so AB = AE (radii of one arc).
Arcs from B and E with one radius meet at F inside ∠DAB. Join A and F.
AB = AE, BF = EF, AF is common, so triangle ABF is congruent to triangle AEF by SSS.
So ∠FAB = ∠FAE, and each is half of 30°, which is 15°.
Slip: arcs from B and D, where AD is not equal to AB, do not give matching triangles.

media.context: Constructions and Tilings. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A six pointed star with a regular hexagon inside it. At each corner of the hexagon a straight line leaves sixty degrees for the triangle, so every point has three sixty degree angles. Keeko's doubt, taking the hexagon angle for the point angle, is struck.

maths_rules: GHIJKL is a regular hexagon, so each of its angles is 120°.
AG lies along the extended side LG and AH along the extended side IH.
∠AGH + ∠LGH = 180° (straight line), so ∠AGH = 180° − 120° = 60°.
In the same way ∠AHG = 180° − 120° = 60°.
The angles of a triangle add to 180°, so ∠GAH = 180° − 60° − 60° = 60°.
All three angles are 60°, so triangle AGH is equilateral; the same reasoning works for the other five points.
Slip: reading ∠AGH as the hexagon angle 120°.

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (special angles), Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (special angles), Q4: Draw a line l and mark a point P anywhere outside the line. Construct a perpendicular to the given line l through P. [Hint: Find a line segment on l whose perpendicular bisector passes through P.]
1. With centre P and a radius large enough, draw an arc that cuts l at two points X and Y. Then PX = PY.
2. P is equally far from X and Y, so P lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
3. With centres X and Y and one radius, draw arcs on the other side of l that meet at Q. Then QX = QY.
4. Join P and Q; PQ meets l at O.
5. ΔPXQ ≅ ΔPYQ by SSS, so ∠XPO = ∠YPO; then ΔPOX ≅ ΔPOY by SAS, so ∠POX = ∠POY = 90°.
6. So PQ is the perpendicular to l through P.
Answer: Cut l at X and Y with an arc from P, then find Q with QX = QY; PQ is the perpendicular bisector of XY (SSS, then SAS), so it is perpendicular to l and passes through P

concepts.concept_name: What tiling means: 4 × 6 and 4 × 7 grids

content.text:
6.2 Tiling
Covering a region using a set of shapes, without gaps or overlaps, is called tiling.
Consider a rectangular grid made of unit squares. We call this a 4 × 6 grid, since it has 4 rows and 6 columns.
Can a 4 × 6 grid be tiled using multiple copies of 2 × 1 tiles? We are allowed to rotate a 2 × 1 tile and use it. (Vertical tile, horizontal tile.)
Here is one way. This is not the only tiling possible.
Can a 4 × 7 grid be tiled using 2 × 1 tiles?

content.text:
Worked example: Can a 4 × 6 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles? Show one way.
1. The grid has 4 × 6 = 24 unit squares, and each tile covers 2, so 12 tiles are needed.
2. Each column has 4 squares, one above another.
3. Two vertical tiles cover one column exactly.
4. Do this for all 6 columns: 6 × 2 = 12 tiles, with no gap and no overlap.
Answer: Yes: 12 vertical tiles, 2 in each column

concepts.concept_name: What tiling means: 4 × 6 and 4 × 7 grids

content.text:
Worked example: Can a 4 × 7 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
1. The grid has 4 × 7 = 28 unit squares, an even number, so 14 tiles would be needed.
2. Each of the 7 columns has 4 squares.
3. Two vertical tiles cover each column.
4. 7 columns use 7 × 2 = 14 tiles, with no gap and no overlap.
Answer: Yes: 14 vertical tiles, 2 in each column

concepts.concept_name: Why a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled

content.text:
What about a 5 × 7 grid?
To see that there is no way to tile a 5 × 7 grid using 2 × 1 tiles, observe that this grid has 35 unit squares. Each tile covers exactly 2 unit squares. Complete the justification.

To see that there is no way to tile a 5 × 7 grid using 2 × 1 tiles, observe that this grid has 35 unit squares. Each tile covers exactly 2 unit squares. Complete the justification.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can you tile 5 × 7 by trying for long enough?
2. Count the squares: 5 × 7 = 35.
3. Any number of tiles covers 2, 4, 6, and so on squares: always an even number.
4. 35 is odd, so no tiling exists; one square would always be left over.

content.text:
Worked example: Prove that a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
1. The grid has 5 × 7 = 35 unit squares.
2. Each tile covers exactly 2 unit squares, with no overlap.
3. So any number of tiles covers an even number of squares.
4. 35 is odd, so it is not a number of squares that tiles can cover exactly.
5. So there is no tiling of the 5 × 7 grid.
Answer: Not possible: tiles always cover an even number of squares, and 35 is odd

concepts.concept_name: Which m × n grids can be tiled?

content.text:
Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles, if both m and n are even? If yes, come up with a general strategy to tile it.
One general strategy for this case is to cover each column with vertical tiles. This is possible because the number of rows is even.
Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles, if one of m and n is even and the other is odd? If yes, come up with a general strategy to tile it.
Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles, if both m and n are odd? Give reasons.

content.text:
1. Predict first: which matters more, the number of rows or the number of columns?
2. If the number of rows is even, every column fills with vertical tiles.
3. If only the number of columns is even, every row fills with horizontal tiles.
4. If both are odd, m × n is odd, so it can never be tiled.

content.text:
Worked example: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if both m and n are even? Give a strategy.
1. Each column has m squares, and m is even.
2. Cover each column with m ÷ 2 vertical tiles.
3. Every column is covered, so the whole grid is covered with no gaps or overlaps.
4. For example, a 6 × 4 grid uses 3 vertical tiles in each of 4 columns, 12 tiles in all.
Answer: Yes: cover each column with vertical tiles

concepts.concept_name: Which m × n grids can be tiled?

content.text:
Worked example: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if one of m and n is even and the other is odd? Give a strategy.
1. If the number of rows m is even, cover each column with vertical tiles, as before.
2. If instead the number of columns n is even, each row has an even number of squares.
3. Then cover each row with n ÷ 2 horizontal tiles.
4. For example, a 3 × 4 grid: each of the 3 rows takes 2 horizontal tiles, 6 tiles in all.
Answer: Yes: use vertical tiles along the even side's columns, or horizontal tiles along rows of even length

concepts.concept_name: Which m × n grids can be tiled?

content.text:
Worked example: Is an m × n grid tileable with 2 × 1 tiles if both m and n are odd? Give reasons.
1. The number of unit squares is m × n.
2. An odd number times an odd number is odd, for example 3 × 5 = 15.
3. Each tile covers 2 squares, so tiles always cover an even number of squares.
4. An odd number of squares can never be covered exactly.
Answer: No: m × n is odd, and tiles always cover an even number of squares

concepts.concept_name: Practice: tile grids or prove it impossible

content.text:
Tiling means no gaps and no overlaps.
An even side lets every column, or every row, fill with tiles.
If both sides are odd, the number of squares is odd, so no tiling exists.

content.text:
Worked example: A 5 × 3 grid (5 rows, 3 columns) has its top right square removed. Can the remaining 14 squares be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
1. 14 squares would need 7 tiles.
2. Top row: the two squares left form one horizontal tile.
3. Rows 2 and 3: put a vertical tile in each of the 3 columns.
4. Rows 4 and 5: put a vertical tile in each of the 3 columns.
5. That is 1 + 3 + 3 = 7 tiles, with no gaps and no overlaps.
Answer: Yes: 1 horizontal tile in the top row and 6 vertical tiles below

content.text:
Worked example: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its second row removed. Can the remaining squares be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles?
1. 14 squares would need 7 tiles.
2. Row 1: the left two squares form one horizontal tile.
3. The top right square goes with the square below it: one vertical tile.

concepts.concept_name: Colour the squares: black and white must match

content.text:
What about this one? Were you able to tile this? How can we be sure that this is not tileable?
Can you find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable?
There is an interesting way to look at these questions. For any tiling problem of this kind, we can create a similar problem with the unit squares coloured black and white so that black squares have only white neighbours and white squares have only black neighbours.
In the black-and-white region, the problem is to tile the region with the 2 × 1 black-and-white tiles so that each black square of a tile sits on a black square of the grid, and each white square sits on a white square.
If the plain grid is tileable, is the black-and-white-grid tileable? If the black-and-white grid is tileable, is the plain grid tileable? It can be seen that the answer to both the questions is yes.
Is the black-and-white region tileable?
Any region tiled with black-and-white-tiles must have an equal number of black tiles and white tiles.
Since the black-and-white region has 8 white squares and 6 black squares, it can never be tiled with these tiles!
Use this idea to find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable?
Isn't it surprising how, by introducing colours and making the problem more complicated, it becomes easier to tackle? What a creative way of looking at the problem!

content.text:
1. Predict first: the grid with the top middle square removed has 14 squares. Can it be tiled?
2. Colour the grid like a chessboard, with the corners white: 8 white and 7 black squares.
3. A 2 × 1 tile always covers two neighbouring squares, one white and one black.
4. Remove a black square and 8 white and 6 black are left; 7 tiles would need 7 of each, so it is impossible.

content.text:
Worked example: A 5 × 3 grid has the middle square of its top row removed. Colour it like a chessboard with white corners, and decide whether it can be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
1. With white corners, the full 5 × 3 grid has 8 white and 7 black squares.
2. The top middle square sits between two white corners, so it is black.
3. After removing it, 8 white and 6 black squares are left.
4. Each 2 × 1 tile covers two neighbouring squares, and neighbours have different colours, so each tile covers one white and one black.
5. 7 tiles would cover 7 white and 7 black squares, but there are 8 white and 6 black.
6. So no tiling exists.
Answer: Not tileable: 8 white and 6 black squares remain, but every tile covers one of each

concepts.concept_name: Colour the squares: black and white must match

content.text:
Worked example: Use the colouring to find another unit square that, when removed from a 5 × 3 grid, makes it non-tileable.
1. Colour the 5 × 3 grid with white corners: 8 white and 7 black squares.
2. Removing any black square leaves 8 white and 6 black, which no set of tiles can cover.
3. The black squares are the ones whose row number plus column number is odd.
4. Besides the top middle square, these are: row 2, column 1; row 2, column 3; row 3, column 2; row 4, column 1; row 4, column 3; row 5, column 2.
5. For example, removing the square in row 2, column 1 makes the grid non-tileable.
Answer: Any black square works, for example row 2, column 1; the others are row 2 column 3, row 3 column 2, row 4 column 1, row 4 column 3 and row 5 column 2

concepts.concept_name: Figure it Out (tiling), Q1

content.text:
Figure it Out (tiling), Q1: Is the following tiling possible? Region to be tiled: 12 unit squares in 4 rows, where the top two rows have 2 squares each, at the left, and the bottom two rows have 4 squares each. Tile: an L shape of 3 unit squares (two squares stacked, with one more square beside the bottom one). The tile may be turned.
1. 12 squares need 4 tiles of 3 squares.

content.text:
Figure it Out (tiling), Q2: Is the following tiling possible? Region to be tiled: an 8 × 8 grid with the top right corner square and the bottom left corner square removed. Tile: 2 × 1.
1. The region has 64 squares minus 2, which is 62 squares, an even number.
2. Colour it like a chessboard. In an 8 × 8 board, the top right and bottom left corners have the same colour, say black.
3. The full board has 32 white and 32 black squares. Removing two black ones leaves 32 white and 30 black.
4. Each 2 × 1 tile covers one white and one black square.
5. 31 tiles would cover 31 of each colour, but the counts are 32 and 30.
6. So the region cannot be tiled.
Answer: Not possible: the two removed corners have the same colour, leaving 32 of one colour and 30 of the other

concepts.concept_name: Squares, triangles and hexagons tile the plane

content.text:
Tiling the Entire Plane
So far we have seen how to tile a given region. What about tiling the entire plane?
Can you think of a shape whose copies can tile the entire plane? Clearly, squares can.
Are there other regular polygons that can tile the plane? What about equilateral triangles?
Tiling with equilateral triangles shows the possibility of tiling with another regular polygon.
A plane can be tiled using regular hexagons as well.

content.text:
1. Predict first: at a corner of a tiling, what must the angles that meet add up to?
2. Squares: 4 × 90 = 360, so four squares meet at each corner.
3. Equilateral triangles: 6 × 60 = 360, so six meet at a corner.
4. Regular hexagons: 3 × 120 = 360, so three meet at a corner.

content.text:
Worked example: Explain why squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons can each tile the whole plane.
1. Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must fill the full 360° with no gap and no overlap.
2. A square has angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360, so four squares fill a corner.
3. An equilateral triangle has angles of 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360, so six triangles fill a corner.
4. A regular hexagon has angles of 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360, so three hexagons fill a corner.
5. Repeating these corners in every direction covers the whole plane.
Answer: Each angle goes into 360° exactly: four 90°, six 60°, three 120°

concepts.concept_name: Tilings in art and in nature

content.text:
A plane can also be tiled using more than one shape, and using non-regular polygons. People such as the great Dutch artist Escher (1898 to 1972), whose works explored mathematical themes such as tiling, have come up with creative ways of tiling a plane with animal shapes!
Mathematicians are still exploring various ways of tiling the plane! One of these tilings was found as recently as 2023.
Have you seen tilings in daily life? They are often used in buildings and in designs. Tilings are found in nature too. The front face of bee hives and some wasp nests are tiled using hexagonal cells!
These cells are used by the insects to keep their eggs, larvae and pupae safe, as well as to store food. Because the region is tiled, no space is wasted.
Scientists still wonder how bees and wasps are able to make hexagonal cells. Next time you see any tiling, pay closer attention to it!
Tiling is still one of the most exciting and active areas of research in geometry.
