maths_rules: Where tiles meet at a corner, their angles must fill the full 360° with no gap and no overlap.
A square has angles of 90°, and 4 × 90 = 360, so four squares fill a corner.
An equilateral triangle has angles of 60°, and 6 × 60 = 360, so six triangles fill a corner.
A regular hexagon has angles of 120°, and 3 × 120 = 360, so three hexagons fill a corner.
Repeating these corners in every direction covers the whole plane.
Slip: circles touch only at single points, and curved gaps are left, so circles do not tile.

concepts.concept_name: What we found about constructions and tilings

content.text:
Summary
A division of a line segment, or any geometrical quantity, into two identical parts is called bisection.
Any point that is of equal distance from the two endpoints of a given line segment lies on its perpendicular bisector. This property can be used to construct the perpendicular bisector using a ruler and compass.
The method of constructing the perpendicular bisector can be modified to draw a 90° angle at any point on a line using only a ruler and compass.
An angle can be bisected and copied using the congruence properties of triangles.
A 60° angle can be constructed using a ruler and compass by constructing an equilateral triangle.
Covering a region using a set of shapes, without gaps or overlaps, is called tiling.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students restate the chapter's constructions with their congruence reasons and the meaning of tiling, and use them on a new question.

objectives.objective_text: Students locate the centres A and B of the eye's arcs by drawing equal-radius arcs from X and Y above and below XY, and explain why AX = AY = BX = BY makes the eye symmetrical.
Students prove that AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY by showing ΔABX ≅ ΔABY by SSS, then ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SAS, and using the straight angle at O to get two 90° angles.
Students explain why other centres C and D with CX = CY = DX = DY lie on the line AB, and justify that any point equally far from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
Students place points that are equally far from X and Y, see that they all fall on one line, and name the congruence conditions that prove the line is the perpendicular bisector.
Students construct the perpendicular bisector of a given segment XY in three steps with an unmarked ruler and a compass, and use it to mark the midpoint of XY.
Students construct the perpendicular bisector of segments of different lengths, test which radius choices still work, and justify each choice with congruent triangles.
Students construct a 90° angle at a point O on a line by marking X and Y equally far from O and drawing one pair of equal arcs, and justify the right angle with SSS.
Students construct 90° angles at given points on lines in different positions, including a point near one end, and give the SSS reason each time.
Students bisect a given angle ∠XOY by marking OA = OB and a point C with AC = BC, and justify that OC is the bisector by the SSS congruence condition.
Students explain why eight equally spaced lines make 45° angles, and construct a 45° angle by bisecting a constructed 90° angle.
Students bisect angles of different sizes, build angles such as 45° and 22.5° by repeated halving, and decide which angles halving can and cannot reach.
Students copy a given angle at A onto a ray from X by drawing equal arcs and transferring the chord BC, and justify ∠A = ∠X by the SSS congruence condition.
Students copy angles of different sizes and orientations onto new rays without measuring, and check each copy by SSS.
Students draw a transversal l through a point B and a line m, copy the angle at A to B as a corresponding angle, and explain why the new line n is parallel to m.
Students construct lines parallel to given lines through given points in different orientations, by copying the corresponding angle each time.
Students explain why six congruent equilateral triangles placed round a centre make a hexagon with equal sides and angles of 120°.
Students find the gap left by six angles round a point using the 360° total, and decide whether a 70° angle fits it.
Students explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines in the hexagon made of six equilateral triangles.
Students fit angle wedges round a point, find each missing gap from the 360° total, and test which wedge fills it exactly.
Students construct a 60° angle at A on a segment AX with two equal arcs, and explain that triangle ABC is equilateral.
Students construct a 120° angle as two 60° angles, and construct regular hexagons of side 4 cm and 5 cm with a ruler and a compass.
Students construct 60° and 120° angles with equal arcs, explain each with an equilateral triangle, and construct regular hexagons of a given side.
Students construct a 30° angle by bisecting a constructed 60° angle, and a 15° angle by bisecting 30°, naming the SSS reason for each bisection.
Students construct a six-pointed star from a regular hexagon and justify that each of its six points is an equilateral triangle by finding its angles.
Students build 30° and 15° by bisection, construct the star, and drop perpendiculars from points outside a line by finding a segment whose perpendicular bisector passes through the point.
Students state what a tiling is and tile 4 × 6 and 4 × 7 grids with vertical and horizontal 2 × 1 tiles.
Students complete the counting argument that a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.
Students decide whether an m × n grid can be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles when both sides are even, one is even, or both are odd, and give a strategy or a reason.
Students tile grids of different sizes with 2 × 1 tiles, or show by counting that a grid cannot be tiled.
Students tile a 5 × 3 grid with a corner square removed, and with the middle square of the second row removed, using 7 tiles.
Students colour a grid like a chessboard, compare black and white counts to prove a region cannot be tiled, and find other squares whose removal makes a 5 × 3 grid non-tileable.
Students colour regions like a chessboard, compare black and white counts, and either tile the region or prove that it cannot be tiled.
Students explain why squares, equilateral triangles and regular hexagons tile the plane, using the angles that meet round a corner.
Students test whether copies of a regular polygon can meet round a corner with no gap, and name the three regular polygons that tile the plane.
Students restate the chapter's constructions with their congruence reasons and the meaning of tiling, and use them on a new question.

Book item: Draw a line segment XY. Construct its perpendicular bisector using only an unmarked ruler and a compass, and mark the midpoint of XY.

Book item: When constructing the perpendicular bisector, is it necessary to have the same radius for the arcs above and below XY? Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer. [Hint 1: Any point that is of the same distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector. Hint 2: We can draw the whole line if any two of its points are known.]

Book item: Draw any angle ∠XOY. Bisect it using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the two parts are equal.

Book item: Construct at least 4 different angles. Draw their bisectors.

Explore this through construction, and then justify your answer.
Book item: What are the other angles that can be constructed using angle bisection? Can you construct 65.5° angle?

Book item: Construct the following figure: a square with four equal petals inside it, each petal running from the centre of the square to one corner. How do we construct the petals so that they are of the maximum possible size within a given square?
Book item: An angle with vertex A is drawn. Copy it onto a ray from a point X using only a ruler and a compass, and justify that the copy is equal.
Book item: Construct at least 4 different angles in different orientations without taking any measurement. Make a copy of all these angles.
Book item: A line m and a point B not on it are given. Construct a line through B parallel to m using only a ruler and a compass.
Book item: Construct 4 pairs of parallel lines in different orientations.

Book item: Angles of 40°, 60°, 50°, 30°, 40° and 90° are placed round a point O, leaving a gap ∠AOI. Find the gap angle. Will a 70° angle fit into the gap?
Book item: In a regular hexagon ABCDEF made of six equilateral triangles round the centre O, explain why AOD, BOE and COF are straight lines.
Book item: Construct a 60° angle at A on a segment AX using only a ruler and a compass, and explain why it is 60°.
Book item: Construct a 120° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
Book item: Construct a regular hexagon with side 4 cm using a ruler and a compass.
Book item: Construct a regular hexagon with side 5 cm using the 120° construction at each corner.
Book item: Construct a 30° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.
Book item: Construct a 15° angle at a point A on a line, using only a ruler and a compass.

Book item: Draw a line l and mark a point P anywhere outside the line. Construct a perpendicular to the given line l through P. [Hint: Find a line segment on l whose perpendicular bisector passes through P.]

Book item: Can a 4 × 6 grid be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles? Show one way.

Book item: Prove that a 5 × 7 grid cannot be tiled with 2 × 1 tiles.

Book item: Is the following tiling possible? Region to be tiled: 12 unit squares in 4 rows, where the top two rows have 2 squares each, at the left, and the bottom two rows have 4 squares each. Tile: an L shape of 3 unit squares (two squares stacked, with one more square beside the bottom one). The tile may be turned.
